Authors Affiliation * 1 Jagiellonian University, Krakow, Poland. * PMID: 24094278 * DOI: 10.1111/bjop.12001 Abstract In contrast to the ample research that shows a positive relationship between the need for closure (NFC) and heuristic information processing, this research examines the hypothesis that this relationship is moderated by the ability to achieve closure (AAC), that is, the ability to use information-processing strategies consistent with the level of NFC. fetched_contents.text: When education fails: Narcissism, uniqueness, and need for closure in conspiracy beliefs and misinformation 1. Introduction Misinformation and conspiracy theories present significant challenges for modern societies, even in highly educated populations. Misinformation is often used as an umbrella term to describe information that is false or misleading, according to the best available evidence (Altay et al., 2023). Conspiracy theories describe a secretive plot undertaken by two or more people that is of public interest, but not public knowledge (Douglas & Sutton, 2023). Education shows consistent protective effects against belief in conspiracy theories, primarily through enhanced analytic reasoning, scientific literacy and improved cognitive abilities (Enders et al., 2024; van Prooijen, 2017). Van Prooijen finds the effect of education on conspiracy theories to be mediated by several factors: including increased sense of control, social class, and cognitive sophistication. These findings support the notion that education, which is widely considered the most common intervention for epistemically unwarranted beliefs, is useful and effective; however, recent research suggests these relationships have important caveats. Findings suggest personality traits and cognitive features interact with education, and in some cases can negate the protective effects that a formal education offers. Under certain conditions, namely in the presence of narcissistic grandiosity, need for uniqueness, and collective narcissism, highly educated individuals are equally likely to endorse conspiracy theories (Cosgrove & Murphy, 2023). Moreover, cognitive reflection showed a protective effect among the highly educated which suggests that those who rely on intuitive thinking see smaller benefits from education than those with a more deliberative cognitive style. The phenomenon of ‘ideologically motivated reasoning’ describes that those with strong numeric and scientific literacy are often the most divided on politically polarised topics (Kahan, 2013; Kahan et al., 2017). Moreover, highly educated individuals are often more willing to express fringe or polarised views on such topics (Lee & Tipoe, 2024), suggesting that highly educated individuals are often more entrenched in beliefs that matter deeply to them. Taken together, these findings suggest the presence of latent cognitive, psychological and ideological needs that override accuracy motivations and reasoning abilities associated with education. Conspiracy theories appeal for epistemic (to provide answers in low information environments), existential (to retain a sense of control and safety) and social reasons (to protect one's image and the image of in-groups; Douglas et al., 2017). As such, it is understandable that grandiosity, need for uniqueness and sociopolitical identities negate the effects of education in some cases. As these traits are associated with desires for certainty, control, and positive social perceptions, education-related abilities may be employed to believe conspiracies that provide answers in uncertain times, feelings of intellectual superiority, and provide reasons for any individual or group shortcomings. 1.1. Education and reasoning Conspiracy theories have unique properties – specifically, that they revolve around a nefarious group exerting some kind of power for a reason unknown to the public (Douglas & Sutton, 2023). It is unclear whether psychological and cognitive needs offset education in conspiracy theories because of these unique properties and associated motivations, or whether these interactions describe a fundamental change in general reasoning abilities. If the latter is true, this would imply that these same effects would also apply to the broader topic of misinformation. Unlike conspiracy theories, misinformation does not necessarily imply nefarious activity by a shadowy out-group and they therefore differ in their psychosocial influences. As such, researchers cannot assume that the same motivations would lead educated individuals to endorse misinformation as they do conspiracy theories. A recent meta-analysis finds a negligible effect of education in discriminating truth from misinformation in online environments (Sultan et al., 2024). This paints a more complex picture and likely reflects the varied nature of misinformation. Belief in misinformation often depends on alignment of content with existing worldviews and social groups (Rathje et al., 2023), as well as the audience's ability to detect persuasive strategies commonly embedded within misinformation (Roozenbeek et al., 2022). As such, further investigation is required into when education protects against misinformation. 1.2. Education and social factors In addition to narcissistic grandiosity and need for uniqueness (Cosgrove & Murphy, 2023), other psychosocial factors may also play a role when education fails to protect against epistemically unwarranted beliefs. Generalised trust and social dominance orientation (support for social hierarchies) are noted as prominent predictors of such (Cichocka et al., 2017; Dyrendal et al., 2021; Gundersen et al., 2024). In the case of trust, it is plausible that existential motivations are activated by strong distrust – that a strong desire to remain safe and in control can supersede accuracy motivations in the face of a perceived threat. Social dominance orientation (SDO) represents a view that intergroup competition and hierarchy are natural, aligning with beliefs that groups naturally conspire for societal position. As such, individuals with a strong SDO may endorse conspiracy theories that threaten their in-groups or preferred authority (Freelon, 2024). Similarly, that this may activate social motivations to protect important in-groups and may also offset the effects of education. 1.3. What need for closure is and why it matters for misinformation acceptance

Need for closure is best understood as a motivated desire for certainty and an intolerance of uncertainty, which drives people to seek closure quickly rather than remaining open to ambiguity [N1-R2] [N1-R3]. The concept is rooted in cognitive psychology and can be operationalized as the need for cognitive closure, a trait-like tendency to prefer structured, predictable, and settled information over open-ended or uncertain information [N1-R2] [N1-R3]. The evidence provided here also emphasizes that this need is not merely passive discomfort; it is an active motivational force that shapes information processing, such as seeking fewer alternative explanations, focusing on initial information, and favoring quick conclusions [N1-R2].

Need for closure matters for misinformation acceptance because it directly influences motivation to resolve uncertainty. People with high need for closure are more likely to jump to conclusions and gather minimal data when making overconfident judgments, which can make them especially susceptible to information that provides a quick, coherent, and certain narrative [N3-R1] [N3-R2]. In the evidence provided, this mechanism is linked to heuristic information processing: high need for closure is associated with more heuristic processing when people believe they can use cognitive strategies consistent with their NFC level, whereas low ability to achieve closure weakens this relationship [N1-F1]. In other words, the need for closure matters not just because people dislike uncertainty, but because it drives them to process information in ways that can easily accept or overweigh false claims.

Why people with high need for closure are more vulnerable to misinformation is therefore tied to both motivation and information-processing style. The evidence suggests that high NFC can lead to premature closure, selective attention, and reliance on simple, intuitive explanations rather than careful evaluation [N1-R2] [N3-R1]. In the context of misinformation, this means that people with high need for closure are more likely to accept false or misleading information if it offers a quick resolution to uncertainty, especially when they perceive the information as providing closure consistent with their cognitive preferences [N1-R2] [N1-F1]. The evidence also points to a broader pattern that need for closure is associated with ideological extremism, conspiracy beliefs, and belief in misleading or false information, which further explains why it is a recurring risk factor for misinformation acceptance [N1-R4] [N1-R5].

Overall, the evidence provided supports a clear causal story: need for closure is a psychological trait rooted in the desire for certainty, it motivates people to resolve uncertainty quickly, and it increases vulnerability to misinformation because it encourages heuristic processing, premature closure, and selective information seeking [N1-R2] [N1-R3] [N3-R1] [N1-F1].

Evidence that need for closure actually predicts acceptance of misinformation

The evidence provided here is strong that need for closure predicts acceptance of false claims and related misinformation-like phenomena, especially in studies on conspiracy beliefs, eyewitness memory, and belief updating. One direct study explicitly states that high need for closure is associated with more heuristic information processing, and in some cases, this relationship is stronger when people believe they can achieve closure effectively [N1-F1]. Another study in the same evidence set extends this logic to conspiracy beliefs and misinformation, noting that education’s protective effect is offset by narcissism, uniqueness, and closure, and that these findings extend prior findings from conspiracy beliefs to misinformation [N2-R1]. That is, the evidence does not simply show correlation; it supports a broader claim that need for closure is a meaningful predictor of acceptance of false or misleading information in real-world contexts [N2-R1].

The dose-response or strength of the effect across populations is somewhat mixed in the provided evidence, but the overall pattern is consistent. The evidence shows that need for closure is associated with ideological extremism, conspiracy beliefs, and belief in real-world conspiracy theories, with the relationship documented in two studies [N1-R4] [N1-R5]. It also shows that in eyewitness situations, need for cognitive closure augments retrieval-induced forgetting, which in turn magnifies misinformation effects [N4-R4]. This suggests that the effect is not always weak or uniform; in some domains, especially those involving memory and eyewitness processing, the effect is substantial and direct [N4-R4]. However, the evidence also includes a broader review of misinformation belief drivers, which notes that the relationship between need for closure and misinformation belief is part of a larger set of factors, including cognitive style and other psychological drivers [N5-F3]. So the evidence supports a moderate to strong effect overall, but not a single universal effect of the same magnitude in every population or context.

As for whether the effect is direct or mediated by other factors, the evidence points to both. On the direct side, need for closure predicts heuristic processing, which in turn predicts acceptance of false information [N1-F1]. On the mediated side, the evidence suggests that personality traits, cognitive style, and other psychological factors can interact with need for closure. For example, the evidence shows that Openness, Extraversion, and Honesty-Humility are negatively predictive of cognitive closure in medical students, suggesting that personality traits can moderate the effect [N4-R2]. The broader review also states that need for cognitive closure and cognitive style are among the psychological drivers of misinformation belief, indicating that these are not isolated predictors but part of a mediated system [N5-F3]. In the context of misinformation acceptance, then, need for closure often acts as a core mechanism, but its influence is frequently amplified or constrained by other cognitive and personality factors.

In short, the evidence supports a robust conclusion: need for closure is a valid predictor of acceptance of false claims and misinformation-related attitudes, with a moderate to strong effect in some populations and domains. The effect is not always direct; it is often mediated by cognitive style, personality, and other information-processing factors [N1-F1] [N2-R1] [N4-R2] [N5-F3].

When need for closure does not explain misinformation acceptance

The evidence provided shows that need for closure does not always explain misinformation acceptance, and in some cases the relationship disappears or even reverses. One key point is that the relationship is moderated by the ability to achieve closure: when participants assess themselves as being able to use cognitive strategies consistent with their NFC level (high AAC), the relationship between NFC and heuristic processing is positive; but when AAC is low, the relationship becomes negative [N1-F1]. This is important because it means that NFC is not a fixed vulnerability; it depends on the person’s ability to use appropriate information-processing strategies. In other words, need for closure can become a liability only when people lack the capacity to satisfy it effectively, and it can become neutral or even protective when they do [N1-F1].

Moderators such as motivation, knowledge, and source credibility are also relevant. The evidence notes that education’s protective effect is offset by narcissism, uniqueness, and closure, but also that other psychosocial factors can negate education’s protection [N2-R1]. In addition, the broader review of misinformation belief drivers emphasizes that belief in misinformation often depends on alignment with existing worldviews and social groups, as well as the audience’s ability to detect persuasive strategies embedded in misinformation [N5-F3]. This implies that motivation and knowledge matter: when people already have strong worldviews or can recognize persuasive tactics, NFC alone may not drive acceptance. Similarly, source credibility plays a role: one study in the evidence set explores whether perceived unreliability of the source providing a retraction leads to higher reliance on misinformation [N6-R3]. That suggests that even if NFC is high, acceptance can be reduced if the source is perceived as trustworthy, or increased if the source is seen as unreliable. In short, NFC is a useful predictor only when the surrounding context is such that people cannot simply ignore uncertainty or evaluate information carefully [N2-R1] [N5-F3] [N6-R3].

Differences across types of misinformation or domains are also apparent. The evidence shows that the relationship is strongest in eyewitness memory and retrieval-induced forgetting contexts, where NFC magnifies misinformation effects [N4-R4]. It also shows that the evidence base includes studies on conspiracy theories, misinformation, and belief updating, but that the effects are not uniform across all types of false information [N2-R1] [N2-R3] [N5-F3]. The broader review notes that the same motivations that apply to conspiracy theories may not apply equally to misinformation, and that misinformation varies in whether it implies nefarious activity or merely false information [N2-F2]. This matters because some misinformation formats are more aligned with closure-seeking than others. For example, fake news presented as trusted news may be more attractive to people with high NFC than abstract false claims, precisely because it mimics trusted sources and offers a ready-made narrative [N4-R5]. Thus, the evidence supports the idea that NFC explains some forms of misinformation acceptance, but not all; the effect is domain-specific and depends on whether the false information fits NFC’s motivational profile [N2-F2] [N4-R4] [N4-R5].

Overall, the evidence provided shows that need for closure does not always explain misinformation acceptance. The effect can disappear or reverse when people have high ability to achieve closure, when motivation or knowledge protects against false information, when source credibility matters, and when the type of misinformation is different from the kinds studied in NFC research [N1-F1] [N2-R1] [N5-F3] [N6-R3] [N4-R4].

What cognitive and personality factors amplify or buffer the need for closure effect

The evidence provided indicates that personality traits and cognitive styles interact with need for closure, either amplifying or buffering its effect on misinformation vulnerability. On the personality side, the evidence explicitly states that Openness, Extraversion, and Honesty-Humility are negatively predictive of medical students’ tendency towards cognitive closure [N4-R2]. This is important because it shows that high need for closure is not a uniform trait; it is associated with certain personality profiles that can either strengthen or weaken the effect. In other words, individuals who are more open, more extraverted, or more honest/humane are less likely to exhibit high cognitive closure, which can buffer the vulnerability that NFC typically brings [N4-R2].

Cognitive styles also matter. The evidence notes that need for cognitive closure is part of a broader set of psychological drivers of misinformation belief, including cognitive style [N5-F3]. It also points to the role of cognitive reflection in some educational research, where cognitive reflection showed a protective effect among highly educated individuals [N2-F2]. This suggests that deliberative thinking can counteract intuitive thinking and reduce the risk of accepting false information, even when NFC is high. In the eyewitness context, need for cognitive closure augments retrieval-induced forgetting, which in turn magnifies misinformation effects [N4-R4]. So cognitive style affects the pathway by which NFC operates: deliberative styles may reduce reliance on heuristics, while intuitive or retrieval-driven styles may increase misinformation vulnerability [N2-F2] [N4-R4].

These factors can either increase or reduce misinformation vulnerability in different ways. Personality traits associated with low cognitive closure can act as buffers because they reduce the motivation to seek closure quickly and therefore reduce the pull of false information [N4-R2]. Cognitive styles that support careful thinking, such as cognitive reflection, can also buffer the effect by promoting more accurate processing and reducing reliance on heuristic shortcuts [N2-F2]. Conversely, personality traits linked to high NFC, such as narcissism, uniqueness, and closure, can amplify the effect by offsetting protective factors such as education [N2-R1]. Similarly, cognitive styles that are more intuitive or less reflective may amplify misinformation vulnerability because they make people more susceptible to retrieval-induced forgetting and quicker closure [N4-R4]. The evidence also suggests that social and motivational factors, such as lack of trust in institutions, can amplify the effect by increasing the importance of closure-seeking in uncertain environments [N4-R3].

In short, the evidence shows that need for closure is not an isolated vulnerability. It is amplified by personality traits such as narcissism and uniqueness, and by cognitive styles that favor intuitive processing, while it is buffered by personality traits such as Openness, Extraversion, and Honesty-Humility, and by cognitive styles that support deliberative reflection [N2-R1] [N4-R2] [N2-F2] [N4-R4]. These factors shape whether high NFC increases misinformation vulnerability, reduces it, or leaves it unchanged [N4-R2] [N2-F2] [N4-R4].

Need for closure is best understood as a motivated desire for certainty and an intolerance of uncertainty, which drives people to seek closure quickly rather than remaining open to ambiguity [N1-R2] [N1-R3]. The concept is rooted in cognitive psychology and can be operationalized as the need for cognitive closure, a trait-like tendency to prefer structured, predictable, and settled information over open-ended or uncertain information [N1-R2] [N1-R3]. The evidence provided here also emphasizes that this need is not merely passive discomfort; it is an active motivational force that shapes information processing, such as seeking fewer alternative explanations, focusing on initial information, and favoring quick conclusions [N1-R2].

Need for closure matters for misinformation acceptance because it directly influences motivation to resolve uncertainty. People with high need for closure are more likely to jump to conclusions and gather minimal data when making overconfident judgments, which can make them especially susceptible to information that provides a quick, coherent, and certain narrative [N3-R1] [N3-R2]. In the evidence provided, this mechanism is linked to heuristic information processing: high need for closure is associated with more heuristic processing when people believe they can use cognitive strategies consistent with their NFC level, whereas low ability to achieve closure weakens this relationship [N1-F1]. In other words, the need for closure matters not just because people dislike uncertainty, but because it drives them to process information in ways that can easily accept or overweigh false claims.

Why people with high need for closure are more vulnerable to misinformation is therefore tied to both motivation and information-processing style. The evidence suggests that high NFC can lead to premature closure, selective attention, and reliance on simple, intuitive explanations rather than careful evaluation [N1-R2] [N3-R1]. In the context of misinformation, this means that people with high need for closure are more likely to accept false or misleading information if it offers a quick resolution to uncertainty, especially when they perceive the information as providing closure consistent with their cognitive preferences [N1-R2] [N1-F1]. The evidence also points to a broader pattern that need for closure is associated with ideological extremism, conspiracy beliefs, and belief in misleading or false information, which further explains why it is a recurring risk factor for misinformation acceptance [N1-R4] [N1-R5].

Overall, the evidence provided supports a clear causal story: need for closure is a psychological trait rooted in the desire for certainty, it motivates people to resolve uncertainty quickly, and it increases vulnerability to misinformation because it encourages heuristic processing, premature closure, and selective information seeking [N1-R2] [N1-R3] [N3-R1] [N1-F1].

The broader review notes that the same motivations that apply to conspiracy theories may not apply equally to misinformation, and that misinformation varies in whether it implies nefarious activity or merely false information [N2-F2]. This matters because some misinformation formats are more aligned with closure-seeking than others. For example, fake news presented as trusted news may be more attractive to people with high NFC than abstract false claims, precisely because it mimics trusted sources and offers a ready-made narrative [N4-R5]. Thus, the evidence supports the idea that NFC explains some forms of misinformation acceptance, but not all; the effect is domain-specific and depends on whether the false information fits NFC’s motivational profile [N2-F2] [N4-R4] [N4-R5].

## 4) Cognitive and personality factors that amplify or buffer the need for closure effect

Cognitive and personality factors interact with need for closure in ways that can either amplify or buffer its effect on misinformation vulnerability. On the personality side, the evidence explicitly states that Openness, Extraversion, and Honesty-Humility are negatively predictive of medical students’ tendency towards cognitive closure [N4-R2]. This means that individuals with these traits are less likely to exhibit high cognitive closure, which can buffer the vulnerability that NFC typically brings [N4-R2]. In other words, personality traits associated with openness, extraversion, and honesty/humility can reduce the pull of misinformation by reducing the motivation to seek closure quickly.

Cognitive styles also matter. The evidence notes that need for cognitive closure is part of a broader set of psychological drivers of misinformation belief, including cognitive style [N5-F3]. It also points to the role of cognitive reflection in some educational research, where cognitive reflection showed a protective effect among highly educated individuals [N2-F2]. This suggests that deliberative thinking can counteract intuitive thinking and reduce the risk of accepting false information, even when NFC is high. In the eyewitness context, need for cognitive closure augments retrieval-induced forgetting, which in turn magnifies misinformation effects [N4-R4]. So cognitive style affects the pathway by which NFC operates: deliberative styles may reduce reliance on heuristics, while intuitive or retrieval-driven styles may increase misinformation vulnerability [N2-F2] [N4-R4].

These factors can either increase or reduce misinformation vulnerability in different ways. Personality traits associated with low cognitive closure can act as buffers because they reduce the motivation to seek closure quickly and therefore reduce the pull of false information [N4-R2]. Cognitive styles that support careful thinking, such as cognitive reflection, can also buffer the effect by promoting more accurate processing and reducing reliance on heuristic shortcuts [N2-F2]. Conversely, personality traits linked to high NFC, such as narcissism, uniqueness, and closure, can amplify the effect by offsetting protective factors such as education [N2-R1]. Similarly, cognitive styles that are more intuitive or less reflective may amplify misinformation vulnerability because they make people more susceptible to retrieval-induced forgetting and quicker closure [N4-R4]. The evidence also suggests that social and motivational factors, such as lack of trust in institutions, can amplify the effect by increasing the importance of closure-seeking in uncertain environments [N4-R3].

## 5) Synthesis

Overall, the role of need for closure in misinformation acceptance is best understood as a motivated information-processing bias. People with high need for closure are more vulnerable to misinformation because they seek closure quickly, rely on heuristic processing, and are more likely to accept information that offers a quick, coherent resolution to uncertainty [N1-R2] [N1-F1] [N3-R1]. The evidence provided here is strong that need for closure predicts acceptance of false claims and related misinformation-like attitudes, but the effect is not universal; it depends on the person’s ability to achieve closure, on the surrounding context, and on other cognitive and personality factors [N1-F1] [N2-R1] [N5-F3] [N4-R4].

The evidence also shows that the effect can disappear or reverse when people have high ability to achieve closure, when motivation or knowledge protects against false information, when source credibility matters, and when the type of misinformation is different from the kinds studied in NFC research [N1-F1] [N2-R1] [N5-F3] [N6-R3] [N4-R4]. At the same time, personality traits such as Openness, Extraversion, and Honesty-Humility, and cognitive styles that support deliberative reflection, can buffer the effect, while traits and styles linked to intuitive or closure-seeking behavior can amplify it [N4-R2] [N2-F2] [N4-R4].

In short: need for closure increases vulnerability to misinformation because it drives quick closure-seeking and heuristic processing; but it does not always do so. The strength of the effect depends on the person, the context, and the type of misinformation, and it can be amplified or buffered by personality and cognitive factors [N1-R2] [N1-F1] [N2-R1] [N4-R2] [N5-F3] [N6-R3].
